Words are easy to remember when you know their first sound and first letter. Say the sounds out loud as you read.
ball → B, cat → C, dog → D
When you meet someone, say **Hello**. When you leave, say **Goodbye**. Say your name with **My name is ...**.
Hello! My name is Mina.
Learn number words like one, two, three... and colour words like red, blue, yellow...
three = 3, red = the colour of a strawberry
mother (mum), father (dad), grandmother (grandma), baby (a very young child): these are words for people in your family.
This is my mother.
desk, chair, bag, pencil, book... Say the things in your classroom in English.
I have a pencil.
Words that name things, like rabbit (an animal with long ears), bird (an animal that flies) and fish (an animal that swims), are called **nouns**.
🐰 = rabbit
Words that show an action, like jump (go up in the air), run (move fast) and eat (have food), are called **verbs**.
I eat an apple.
**I like ...** means you enjoy something. **I have ...** means something is yours.
I like dogs. I have a cat.
After I, use **am**. After You, use **are**. A sentence goes in this order: 'who → what they are / what they do'.
I am a student. You are kind.
When you read, first look for the words from the question in the text.
Mina has a cat. → a cat
A sentence goes in this order: 'who → does → what'. After He, She or a person's name, add **-s** to the verb.
She reads a book.
Instead of a name, you can use **He**, **She**, **It**, **They** or **We**.
Tom is tall. He is tall.
For things happening now or again and again, use the **present**. For things that already happened, use the **past**: add **-ed** to the end of the verb.
I walk. → I walked.
get up, brush my teeth, eat breakfast, go to bed... Say your daily routine in English.
I get up at seven.
Read the text and find who did what, and when.
Jin gets up at seven.
For now or habits, use the **present**. For the past, add **-ed**. For things you will do, use **will + base verb**.
I will visit my aunt tomorrow.
Start a question with **Do/Does**. To say no, use **don't/doesn't**.
Do you like pizza? I don't like onions.
Words like big, small, hot and cold describe how something looks or feels.
The ice cream is cold.
Use **on**, **in**, **under** and **behind** to say where things are.
The book is on the desk.
Find who did what, and where, in the text, then answer.
Mina goes to the park.
Use **an** before a vowel sound and **a** before a consonant sound. For one thing, use **There is**. For many things, use **There are**.
an apple, two boxes, There are three books.
To compare two things, use **-er + than**. For 'the most', use **the -est**. For long words, use **more**.
Tom is taller than Ben.
For things you will do, use **will + base verb** or **be going to + base verb**.
I am going to visit Jeju.
For negatives, use **not / don't / doesn't / didn't**. For questions, put **Are / Do / Does** at the start of the sentence.
I am happy. → I am not happy.
Long texts are easier if you find who, where, when and what, as if you were underlining them.
Ken lives in Busan.
For things happening now, use **be + -ing**. For the past, use the **past tense**. For the future, use **will / be going to**.
The baby is sleeping now.
**can** (be able to), **must** (have to), **should** (it is a good idea to), **may** (it is OK to) are followed by the base form of the verb.
You should brush your teeth.
Learn words with similar meanings and opposites together, and your vocabulary will double.

Join sentences with **because** (reason), **so** (result), **but** (contrast), **if** (condition) and **when** (time).

Read a text with several sentences and find who did something, when and why.

had + p.p. is for something that happened before another past event. have been -ing is for an action that has continued until now.

Drop the conjunction and the subject, and change the verb to -ing. The subject must be the same in both parts.

Tell apart cause and effect (so, therefore), contrast (however), examples (for example) and addition (in addition).
However = but, on the other hand
The main idea is often after However, which turns a common belief around, and in the last sentence. Fill in a blank by following the flow problem → solution → result.

When Never/Hardly/Only then comes first, the order becomes auxiliary + subject. Use It is ~ that for emphasis.
Never have I seen such a view.
In I wish / as if / If clauses, use the past for the opposite of the present and had p.p. for the opposite of the past.

whatever, whoever, whichever and however + adjective mean 'no matter what / who / which / how ...'.

The verb be: am / are / is
The verb be changes its form with the subject. **I → am**, **he / she / it → is**, **you / we / they → are**.
I am a student. She is my friend. They are in the classroom.
When the subject is **he / she / it (third person singular)**, add **-s / -es** to the verb. Words ending in -ch, -sh, -s, -x, -o take -es. For consonant + y, change y to i and add -es!
go → goes / watch → watches / study → studies
Plurals and building sentences
For two or more, usually add **-s** to the noun. Nouns ending in -x take **-es**. Learn irregular plurals by heart. A sentence goes **subject → verb → the rest**.
book → books / box → boxes / child → children
have/has + past participle. It shows experience, completion or continuation. Tell since (a point in time) apart from for (a length of time).
I have lived here for five years.
Use be + past participle to say that something is done to someone or something. Add the doer with by.
The room is cleaned by Mina.
want, hope, decide + to-infinitive; enjoy, finish, avoid + gerund. stop + to V shows purpose, and stop + V-ing means stopping an action.
I want to buy a bike. She enjoys singing.
-er/-est and more/most. Use than with comparatives and the with superlatives. good → better → best is irregular.
hot → hotter → the hottest
Read the question first, then find the clue sentence. The title and main idea cover the whole text.
As a result = because of this
Join two sentences into one with who (people), which (things), that (both) and whose (possession).
I have a friend who lives in Canada.
If + present, will + V (something possible). If + past, would + V (imagining something that is not true now).
If I were rich, I would travel.
Use the order question word + subject + verb. Do not use do/does/did.
Do you know where he lives?
-ing is active or ongoing; -ed is passive or finished. For feelings, use -ing for what causes the feeling and -ed for the person who feels it.
an exciting game / I am excited
Put clues together to make an inference. Decide the purpose of a text by looking at its requests and claims.
Could you tell me ...? → a question (an inquiry)
Choosing What Fits the Situation

In conversation questions, check not only that the grammar is correct but also that the tone sounds natural and polite in that situation. Offers, interrupting, responding to compliments, idioms and indirect speech come up often.
Workplace Expressions and Collocations

In workplace English, the key points are idioms (touch base), abbreviations (ASAP, etc.) and verb-preposition pairs (collocations). Don't translate word for word; remember them as chunks used in work situations.
Reading Information Critically

In media English, it is important to tell facts from opinions and to judge whether the reasoning in a claim is sound. Remember terms such as image descriptions (alt text, caption) and editing tools by their purpose.
Cultural Vocabulary and an Open Mind

For world-culture topics, learn key words such as culture, diversity and stereotype, and expressions for trying to understand other cultures without judging them. Tell look-alike words apart using context clues.
Reading Works with Literary Terms
In literature questions, the key is to know the definition of a term and apply it to a scene in the story. Keep foreshadowing, symbol, point of view, theme and character roles distinct.
Sorting Out Arguments and Fallacies
Debate requires telling terms (motion, rebuttal, etc.), kinds of evidence and logical fallacies apart. When evaluating a claim, first ask, "What is the evidence for this?"
Accurate Writing That Fits Its Purpose

In writing, choose the form that fits the purpose and the reader, and check sentence components (subject and verb) and the logic of connectors. For specific texts like a resume, actions and numbers are better than vague words.
The alphabet has **capital letters** and **lowercase letters**. Many pairs look different, so learn them one pair at a time. Take special care with letters that look alike, such as b, d, p and q.
A–a, B–b, D–d, G–g
The first sound of a word is linked to its first letter. Find words that begin with the same sound to learn how sounds and spelling are related. Sometimes two letters, such as ph, make the f sound.
cat → cup, fish → fan
Words that show order, such as **First**, **Then / Next**, **After that** and **Finally**, tell you the order in which things happened.
First, I wake up. Then I eat breakfast. Finally, I go to school.

A sentence starts with a **capital letter** and ends with the right **punctuation mark**: a period (.) for a statement, a question mark (?) for a question, and an exclamation mark (!) for surprise or strong feeling. People's names and the word I are always capitalised.
Is this your bag? Yes, it is.

To summarise, find the **main idea** and shrink it to one or two sentences. A sentence about only one detail, one that adds something not in the passage, or one that is too broad is not a good summary.
Recycling saves resources and reduces trash.

Choose the word that fits the blank: I like carrots. → I ____ like carrots.

the tallest is the person with the greatest height.

Choose the right words for the blank in the dialogue. A: What are you going to do this weekend? B: I ____ visit my grandparents.
be going to always needs a be verb.

Use am + going to + base verb, like I am going to visit ...
Choose the word that fits the blank: Look at the dark clouds. It ____ soon.

be verb sentences and action verb sentences make questions in different ways.
run is an action verb.

because tells us why.

so means 'and that is why'.

but shows a contrast.

Choose the word that fits the blank: I ____ swim.

can means 'be able to'.

Choose the word that fits the blank: You ____ be quiet in the library.
must means 'have to'.

Choose the word that fits the blank: ____ I open the window?

May I open ...? = Is it OK if I open ...?
May I open the window? = Is it OK if I open the window?
Choose the word that fits the blank: You ____ brush your teeth every day.
should means 'it is a good idea to'.

You should brush your teeth. = It is a good idea to brush your teeth every day.
Tap the words in the right order to make a sentence. (Meaning: running is not allowed here.)

must not means 'it is not allowed'.

Choose the word that fits the blank: He ____ speak English well.
He can speak English well. = He is good at speaking English.
Choose the word that fits the blank: She ____ play the piano.

She can play the piano. = She is able to play the piano.
Choose the word that fits the blank: You ____ drink more water.

You should drink more water. = It is a good idea to drink more water.

Read the text and answer. "Last Saturday, Jina and her brother went to a science museum. They saw a big dinosaur and learned about space. Jina was tired because they walked a lot, but she was very happy. Next weekend, they are going to visit a zoo." Question: What did they see?

Read the text and answer. "Last Saturday, Jina and her brother went to a science museum. They saw a big dinosaur and learned about space. Jina was tired because they walked a lot, but she was very happy. Next weekend, they are going to visit a zoo." Question: Who went to the museum with Jina?

Choose the word that fits the blank: Look! The baby ____ now.

The present continuous is be + -ing.
The baby is sleeping now. = The baby is asleep at this moment.
Choose the word that fits the blank: I ____ my homework last night.
last night means 'yesterday evening'. It is the past.
The past form of do is did.
I did my homework. = I finished my homework.
Choose the word that fits the blank: She usually ____ at six.
usually means 'most of the time'. It is a habit.
The subject is She, so add -s to the verb.

Write the word that fits the blank: They are ____ in the park now. (play)

Choose the word that fits the blank: By next year, I ____ 13 years old.
next year means 'the year after this one'. It is the future.
will be means 'is going to become'.

Choose the word that fits the blank: He ____ breakfast every day.

yesterday is in the past.

last night tells you the tense.
